posts.note: Review of the Mughal et al. 2025 meta-analysis on therapeutic interventions after adolescent self-harm. Mostly evidence summary; logged hedged calls about future research, hospital practice, payer behaviour and funding.
Review of the Bahadori et al. 2025 meta-analysis of TMS in anorexia nervosa; includes a firm payer-denial prediction and hedged efficacy calls.
135-word podcast announcement; only an implied part-two release.

Rerun of an older medical-education post. Habitual 'will' statements about training (e.g. 'Neurosurgeons won't', 'Most of the people who take that test will not get into medical school') read as generalizations and were not logged; one aphorism and one private-equity aside were.
Personal essay about a dentist and online harassment; two personal calendar/expectation items.
Parenting essay; two low-value personal/advice items.
ADHD sleep explainer; clinical mechanism claims and treatment advice only, no forward-looking calls. Mentions Pear Therapeutics' Somryst in the present tense.
DBS for OCD overview; one hedged practice-adoption call and one own-activity item.
Memoir essay and GoFundMe appeal; no forward-looking statements.

statements.quote: An important note: I'm highly dubious that, absent a much larger data set, we would see a difference.
statements.context: Discussion of the Mughal/Young et al. 2025 meta-analysis (JCPP Advances) of therapeutic interventions after adolescent self-harm. The pooled data showed no difference in mortality. The author doubts that a mortality difference would appear in future work unless the data set were much larger, because death and suicide are rare outcomes in youth.
statements.note: Doubt about a future research readout; conditional on data set size.

statements.quote: The good news is that we could do these psychotherapeutic things in hospitals, and they might be effective.
statements.context: After stating there is no evidence that medication-focused psychiatric hospitalization saves the lives of youth after self-harm, the author says the psychotherapies covered by the meta-analysis could be delivered inside hospitals and might be effective there.
statements.note: Hedged claim about a possible practice change; no timeline.

statements.quote: Of course, there is a corollary: They may not want to pay for care that doesn't work, and honestly, I think that's a good idea.
statements.context: Follows the line 'We need to get insurance companies to actually pay for this sort of care' (specialized psychotherapy for self-harming youth). The author expects insurers may refuse to pay for non-specialized, ineffective care, and endorses that.
statements.note: The preceding sentence is a normative call for insurers to pay; this part is the hedged expectation about payer behaviour.

statements.quote: We should be profoundly ashamed that we have not created any brain-based interventions that met the bar for reducing self-harm and suicide, and we should diligently work to do so. This also will take funding.
statements.context: Closing section: no biological (drug or device) intervention met the inclusion criteria of the meta-analysis. The author calls for developing brain-based interventions for youth self-harm and says this will require funding.
statements.note: Mostly a normative call; the forward-looking part is 'This also will take funding'. Near-truism, low forecast value.

statements.quote: We know that we need to include families in the specialized therapies for self-harming youth , and if we do both of those things, we can reduce the rate of suicide attempts.
statements.context: Summary of the meta-analysis findings: group therapy alone is not enough and family involvement is needed. Conditional claim that doing both (specialized therapy plus family inclusion) reduces suicide attempts.
statements.note: Borderline: a conditional capability claim derived from the meta-analysis rather than a dated forecast. Logged for recall; low forecast value.

statements.quote: One of the very exciting things about working on the sharpest part of the bleeding edge of neuromodulation is how fast and furious new data is coming about, and since these methods are safe, able to change practice rapidly.
statements.context: Opening line of the post on TMS for anorexia nervosa. The author claims that new neuromodulation data, because the methods are safe, can change clinical practice rapidly.
statements.note: General claim about the pace of practice change from neuromodulation data; borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: With transcranial magnetic stimulation, we might have a new effective treatment toolkit!
statements.context: Introducing the Bahadori et al. 2025 meta-analysis (Eating and Weight Disorders) of TMS in anorexia nervosa (9 studies, 129 participants). The author suggests TMS might become a new effective treatment for anorexia nervosa.
statements.note: Hedged efficacy/adoption call for TMS in anorexia nervosa.

statements.quote: For scientists, clinicians, and patients struggling with AN, rTMS seems like a promising option.
statements.context: Conclusion after reviewing the meta-analysis results (marginal BMI gain, larger EDE-Q effect, the TIARA trial as the largest study). The author judges rTMS a promising option for anorexia nervosa (AN).
statements.note: Present-tense appraisal with an implied expectation of future clinical use; borderline.

statements.quote: Of course, this means that it will be submitted— and denied—by most payors because there is no FDA label, and even if there were, it would still be considered experimental and unproven, much like parachutes.
statements.context: Immediately after calling rTMS a promising option for anorexia nervosa. The author predicts that most payors will deny rTMS claims for anorexia because there is no FDA label, and that even with a label payors would still treat it as experimental and unproven.
statements.note: Compound claim: denial by most payors, plus continued 'experimental' status even if FDA labeled. 'Much like parachutes' is sarcasm; the claim reads as sincere.

statements.quote: However, perhaps for my readers working hard every day at payors, at the very least, it might be time to remove Anorexia Nervosa as an exclusionary criterion and allow patients with depression and anorexia to avail themselves of what might be a helpful treatment?
statements.context: Appeal to payer employees to stop excluding anorexia nervosa from TMS coverage for patients who also have depression. The author calls TMS 'what might be a helpful treatment'. Followed by 'I know, I know, but a guy can hope?'.
statements.note: Wish/advice to payers with no prediction that they will act; contains a hedged efficacy claim. Logged for recall with normative flag.

statements.quote: This is part one of a two-part conversation, and thank you for reading, and thank you for listening.
statements.context: Announcement of the author's appearance on Greg Malzberg's PsychoFarm podcast (YouTube), recorded the day before. Part one is out; a part two is implied to follow.
statements.note: Own-content announcement; implies a second episode will be released. Low forecast value; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: About half of what you learn will turn out to be wrong, later; because science progresses. You just don’t know which half.
statements.context: Rerun of an older post on medical education (neurosurgeons and adult ADHD). In the section on the basic science curriculum, the author asserts that about half of what medical students learn will later prove wrong.
statements.note: Common aphorism about medical knowledge; near-truism, low forecast value. Post is a rerun of an earlier article.

statements.quote: You don’t learn why private equity is going to buyer clinic later, or why it’s a terrible idea to have anything to do with that.
statements.context: Footnote 4, on the gap in healthcare economics and business teaching in medical school. The author asserts that private equity is going to buy the future doctor's clinic later. 'buyer clinic' is a typo for 'buy your clinic'.
statements.note: Sardonic footnote aside; reads as a sincere expectation that private equity will acquire physician clinics. Post is a rerun.

statements.quote: This Thursday, we have the next hearing in that court case.
statements.context: Closing of the essay about dentist Dr. Jonathan Okon. The author says he filed a suit against the mother of a former patient who has harassed him for years, and that the next hearing is this Thursday (post dated Friday 2025-02-07).
statements.note: Own legal-calendar item; low forecast value.

statements.quote: It doesn't matter what the problem is with my teeth; Dr. Okon will ensure I'm OK.
statements.context: Personal expectation about the author's dentist, Dr. Jonathan Okon, after the story of daily lidocaine injections for dry socket: whatever the future dental problem, Dr. Okon will take care of it.
statements.note: Personal expectation, not a market or clinical forecast; low value.

statements.quote: We don't have a regular family dinner every other night all week, sure , because between the two doctors who are these children's parents, there's just no way that's gonna happen anytime soon.
statements.context: Parenting essay. The author says his household has Sunday dinner but no regular weeknight family dinner, and predicts that will not change anytime soon because both parents are doctors.
statements.note: Personal household prediction; low forecast value.

statements.quote: But show up for something, no matter how literally pedestrian, regularly. That way, when it matters, you will have some credibility.
statements.context: Closing advice to fathers: do something with your kids regularly (the author walks his twins to school every day). Conditional prediction that regular presence yields credibility when the important moments come.
statements.note: Parenting advice with a conditional predictive reading; generic life claim, low forecast value.

statements.quote: In psychiatry, maybe as our field embraces circuit-based explanations, it’s possible we will get more comfortable embracing durable circuit-based therapeutics like DBS?
statements.context: Conclusion of an overview of deep brain stimulation for OCD (FDA humanitarian device exemption; Graat/Figee 2017 and Dufault 2025 meta-analyses). The author suggests psychiatry may adopt circuit-based therapeutics such as DBS more widely as circuit-based explanations take hold.
statements.note: Hedged and phrased as a question; reads as a sincere tentative expectation about practice adoption.

statements.quote: I’m headed to a consultation with one of my patients in the very near future. Stay tuned.
statements.context: Final lines of the DBS overview. The author says he will soon attend a DBS consultation with one of his patients and signals follow-up coverage in the newsletter.
statements.note: Own-activity announcement; implies a future newsletter follow-up. Low forecast value; coder may mark CONTROL.
